x: Harwood and Matthews of Guildford made it quite clear at the start that they had no intention of relinquishing their unbeaten record, especially on their home course, but Hampshire and Cocks had other ideas.

What ease of mind he had could not have been improved when after 10 Kilos he passed team-mate Matthews, who had dropped back from a 19secs lead to fifth place in a state of exhaustion, and was indeed taken to hospital shortly afterwards.
The "Hurdlers Strike" obviously favoured Trevor Tolson and Alan Spicer (Hildreth and Matthews withdrew claiming that the fierce 30 mph wind was to great to run into).
The manner in which he did this was truly heroic, for his opposition included a peak-form Matthews and five East Germans: all reputed to be very fast, which indeed they were.
However, only 3 men proved themselves better on the day; these were the near-invincible Matthews (49.43.6), Ilford's Williams (53.08.1) and Cambridge Harriers' Godbeer (53.20).

Ray Middleton finished a meritorious third behind Williams and Arthur Thomson of Metropolitan. In all fairness, however, we must admit that the redoubtable Matthews was disqualified at 3¾ miles when leading by 52 secs.
"Yes" said he, "in 1960 a chap called Matthews and a chap called Vickers in the A.A.A.'s 2 miles at the White City." He then went on to give me a blow by blow account of it and it was all correct.

For those of you who have been brought up on a different account of events I prefer the British report which, correctly, states that it was Matthews who finished up in hospital after retiring at halfway.
